Game Finder vs Discovery Wheel — two ways to filter the same catalog

Both tools filter the current game-fact list, but their controls and outputs differ. Neither learns a player profile or ranks games by quality.

By NoCharge Editorial·Reviewed by NoCharge Editorial·Published August 27, 2026·Updated November 24, 2026·2 min read
Check the current platform.

Use the public pages behind this explanation.

Open the ArcadeReview PrivacyKeyboard-only play notes

Bottom line: Game Finder and Discovery Wheel read the same tool-owned facts about published games, but they expose different filters. Their results are matches, not personalized recommendations or popularity rankings.

Game Finder: five grouped questions

Game Finder lets you choose a session limit, player mode, pace, input preference, and broad kind (logic or numbers, memory, or quick round). It intersects the selected answers with the current fact list and sorts matches alphabetically. A “keyboard-complete” result is a catalog fact about the game’s core loop, not a guarantee about your keyboard or assistive technology. Its mouse-or-touch choice accepts either listed pointer or touch support.

Discovery Wheel: four direct filters

Discovery Wheel exposes session limit, players, input, and pace as separate controls. It shows up to three matches and rotates through the matching list when you spin; it has no broad game-kind filter. A session limit compares against the maximum of the tool’s estimated range. These ranges are planning estimates, not measured play times.

What the tools do not do

Neither tool reads a play history, remembers answers for a profile, or assigns a quality score. A result can be empty when no current fact matches every selected constraint. Broaden a filter rather than assuming that one was silently ignored.

Try Game Finder or Discovery Wheel to inspect the current interface and results.
